newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OAU agrees to act on Sierra Leone and former Zaire.
newsitem.headline: OAU agrees to act on Sierra Leone and former Zaire.

text.p: African leaders resolved on Tuesday to isolate the rebel government in Sierra Leone and to help rebuild the former Zaire.

Delegates said speakers during a marathon closed session on the second day of the Organisation of African Unity summit were unanimous in condemning the May 25 military coup against civilian President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah of Sierra Leone.

"We resolved to continue to support the ECOWAS (Economic Community for West African States) action in Freetown and agreed that no one would have anything to do with the council appointed by the coup-makers," said one Southern African delegate.
ECOWAS forces led by Nigeria pounded the city of Freetown from the sea on Monday and took control of two strategic airports in bid to break the coup.

Sierra Leone's ambassador to the United Nations, James Jonah, said in an interview on Tuesday he was confident of an early end to the coup, which he said had been carried out by "thugs and rabble rousers".
"The Nigerian action has our full support," said another delegate to the OAU session, who asked not to be named.
The OAU members also offered full support to President Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo, the former Zaire, which has been left bankrupt after 32 years of Mobutu Sese Seko's dictatorship.

"Everyone agreed that we must do everything we can to help rebuild the former Zaire. The country has been left with nothing, no money, no infrastructure and no effective government," one delegate told Reuters.

He said no one raised doubts in the OAU session about Kabila's commitment to democracy and elections, which he has promised to stage in 1999, and no one referred to the reported massacre and ill-treatment of refugees in the east of the country.
Kabila left before the debate on his takeover of Africa's third largest country, leaving his Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha to represent him.
"I am very happy with the outcome of the debate. It was important because we need all the help we can get now to rebuild the country," Karaha told Reuters.
He said the form of the OAU's support had still to be decided, but he said he expected a South African task force to visit the country soon to look at ways of helping.

Kabila, who dozed off during the opening session of his first OAU summit on Monday, spent most of his two days in Harare in private meetings with other African leaders and U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan.

Annan told a news conference that Kabila had undertaken to appoint a minister in his administration as a contact for the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, and to facilitate access to the refugees.
One delegate said the tone of the closed meeting must have made some of Africa's longer-serving or less democratic leaders uncomfortable.
"The general tone is that Africa is done with despots and dictators. Democracy's time has come," the delegate said.
The summit convenes for a final session on Wednesday and will adopt a communique likely to reflect the debate in Tuesday's closed meeting.
